edition.copy_text: Koetschau, GCS 2–3 (1899), via the Perseus TEI

source_text: Ἡμεῖς μὲν οὖν οὔ φαμεν τὸ διαφθαρὲν σῶμα ἐπανέρχεσθαι εἰς τὴν ἐξ ἀρχῆς φύσιν, ὡς οὐδὲ τὸν διαφθαρέντα „κόκκον“ τοῦ „σίτου“ ἐπανέρχεσθαι εἰς τὸν „κόκκον“ τοῦ „σίτου.“ λέγομεν γὰρ, ὥσπερ ἐπὶ τοῦ κόκκου τοῦ „σίτου“ ἐγείρεται στάχυς. οὕτως λόγος τις ἔγκειται τῷ σώματι, ἀφ᾿ οὗ μὴ φθειρομένου „ἐγείρεται“ τὸ σῶμα „ἐν ἀφθαρσίᾳ.“ οἱ μέντοι ἀπὸ τῆς Στοᾶς τὸ πάντῃ διαφθαρὲν σῶμά φασιν ἐπανέρχεσθαι εἰς τὴν ἐξ ἀρχῆς φύσιν διὰ τὰ δεδογμένα αὐτοῖς περὶ τῶν κατὰ περίοδον ἀπαραλλάκτων, καὶ αὐτὴν ἐκείνην, ἐξ ἧς ἐλύθη, τὴν πρώτην σύστασιν πάλιν φασὶ συστήσεσθαι, διαλεκτικαῖς (ὡς οἴονται) ἀνάγκαις ταῦτα παριστάντες. καὶ οὐκ εἰς ἀτοπωτάτην γε ἀναχώρησιν ἀναχωροῦμεν λέγοντες ὅτι πᾶν δυνατὸν τᾷ θεῷ· οἴδαμεν γὰρ ἀκούειν τοῦ πᾶν οὐκ ἐπὶ τῶν ἀνυπάρκτων οὐδ᾿ ἐπὶ τῶν ἀδιανοήτων. φαμὲν δὲ καὶ ὅτι οὐ δύναται αἰσχρὰ ὁ θεὸς, ἐπεὶ ἔσται ὁ θεὸς δυνάμενος μὴ εἶναι θεός· εἰ γὰρ αἰσχρόν τι δρᾷ θεὸς, οὐκ ἔστι θεός. ἐπεὶ δὲ τίθησιν ὅτι καὶ τὰ παρὰ φύσιν ὁ θεὸς οὐ βούλεται, διαστελλόμεθα τὸ λεγόμενον· ὅτι εἰ μὲν παρὰ φύσιν τὴν κακίαν τις λέγει, καὶ ἡμεῖς λέγομεν ὅτι οὐ βούλεται τὰ παρὰ φύσιν ὁ θεὸς, οὔτε τὰ ἀπὸ κακίας οὔτε τὰ ἀλόγως γινόμενα· εἰ δὲ τὰ κατὰ λόγον θεοῦ καὶ βούλησιν αὐτοῦ γινόμενα, ἀναγκαῖον εὐθέως εἶναι μὴ παρὰ φύσιν· οὐ (γὰρ) παρὰ φύσιν τὰ πραττόμενα ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ, κἂν παράδοξα ᾖ ἢ δοκοῦντά τισι παράδοξα. εἰ δὲ χρὴ βεβιασμένως ὀνομάσαι, ἐροῦμεν ὅτι ὡς πρὸς τὴν κοινοτέραν νοουμένην φύσιν ἐστί τινα ὑπὲρ τὴν φύσιν, ἃ ποιήσαι ἄν ποτε θεὸς, ὑπὲρ τὴν ἀνθρωπίνην φύσιν ἀναβιβάζων τὸν ἄνθρωπον καὶ ποιῶν αὐτὸν μεταβάλλειν ἐπὶ φύσιν κρείττονα καὶ θειοτέραν καὶ τηρῶν τοιοῦτον, ὅσον καὶ ὁ τηρούμενος δι᾿ ὧν πράττει παρίστησιν ὅτι βούλεται.
thought_title: The seed, the Stoics, and what God can do
pass_a_gloss: We (ἡμεῖς) do not say (οὔ φαμεν) the corrupted body (διαφθαρὲν σῶμα, διαφθείρω) returns (ἐπανέρχεσθαι) to its from-the-beginning nature (εἰς τὴν ἐξ ἀρχῆς φύσιν), as neither the corrupted grain (κόκκος) of wheat (σῖτος) returns to the grain of wheat. For we say, as from the grain of wheat an ear (στάχυς) is raised (ἐγείρεται), so a certain principle (λόγος τις) lies in (ἔγκειται) the body, from which, not being corrupted (μὴ φθειρομένου), the body is raised in incorruption (ἐν ἀφθαρσίᾳ). The Stoics (οἱ ἀπὸ τῆς Στοᾶς), however, say the body wholly (πάντῃ) corrupted returns to its original nature, because of their doctrines (δεδογμένα) about things unvarying (ἀπαραλλάκτων) according to period/cycle (κατὰ περίοδον); and that very first constitution (πρώτη σύστασις), from which it was dissolved (ἐλύθη, λύω), they say will be constituted again (συστήσεσθαι), establishing (παριστάντες) these by dialectical necessities (διαλεκτικαῖς ἀνάγκαις), as they think. And we do not withdraw into a most absurd retreat (ἀτοπωτάτη ἀναχώρησις) saying all is possible (πᾶν δυνατὸν) to God; for we know to hear 'all' not of non-existent things (ἀνυπάρκτων) nor of inconceivable things (ἀδιανοήτων). We say also that God cannot (οὐ δύναται) do shameful things (αἰσχρά), since God will be one able not to be God; for if God does (δρᾷ) something shameful, he is not God. Since he posits (τίθησιν) that God does not will (οὐ βούλεται) things contrary to nature (παρὰ φύσιν), we distinguish (διαστελλόμεθα) the saying: if one calls wickedness (κακία) contrary to nature, we also say God does not will things contrary to nature, neither things from wickedness nor things done irrationally (ἀλόγως); but if (one means) things done according to God's reason (κατὰ λόγον θεοῦ) and his will (βούλησις), it is necessary at once that they are not contrary to nature; for the things done by God are not contrary to nature, even if paradoxical (παράδοξα) or seeming paradoxical to some. If one must name in a forced way (βεβιασμένως), we will say that relative to the more commonly understood nature there are some things above nature (ὑπὲρ τὴν φύσιν), which God might sometime do, lifting up (ἀναβιβάζων) man above human nature and making him change (μεταβάλλειν) to a better (κρείττονα) and more divine (θειοτέραν) nature and keeping (τηρῶν) him such, as long as the one kept also shows through what he does that he wills (βούλεται).

pass_b_english: We, then, do not say that the corrupted body returns “to its original nature,” any more than the corrupted grain of wheat returns to being a grain of wheat (1 Corinthians 15:37; John 12:24). For we say that, just as an ear rises from the grain of wheat, so a certain principle lies within the body; and from this principle, which is not corrupted, the body “is raised in incorruption” (1 Corinthians 15:42).

The Stoics, however, say that the body “wholly corrupted” returns “to its original nature,” because of the doctrines they hold about things that recur without variation in each cycle; and they say that “that very first make-up from which it was dissolved” will be put together again, establishing these things, as they suppose, by the necessities of logic.

Nor do we retreat to “a most absurd refuge” when we say that “everything is possible to God” (Matthew 19:26; Mark 10:27). For we know how to understand that “everything”: it does not refer to things that have no existence, nor to things that cannot be conceived. We say, too, that God cannot do shameful things, since then God would be able not to be God; for if God does anything shameful, he is not God.

But since Celsus lays it down that God does not will “what is against nature” either, we draw a distinction in what is said. If someone calls wickedness against nature, we too say that God does not will what is against nature, neither what springs from wickedness nor what happens without reason. But if one means what happens in accordance with God’s reason and his will, then such things must at once be not against nature; for what God does is not against nature, even if it is extraordinary, or seems extraordinary to some.

And if we must use a forced term, we will say that, compared with nature as it is more commonly understood, there are some things above nature which God might at some time do: raising man above human nature, causing him to change into a better and more divine nature, and keeping him so, as long as the one so kept also shows by his deeds that he wills it.
notes: Origen answers Celsus's words quoted at 5.14; phrases lifted verbatim from that passage ('to its original nature', 'wholly corrupted', 'that very first make-up from which it was dissolved', 'a most absurd refuge', 'everything is possible to God', 'what is against nature') are set in double quotation marks as Celsus's words, though Koetschau does not mark them, and they follow the wording used for 5.14 in this translation. διαφθαρέν and φθειρομένου rendered with 'corrupted' so that the link to 'incorruption' (1 Corinthians 15:42) and to Celsus's 'wholly corrupted' stays visible. παρὰ φύσιν rendered 'against nature' throughout, matching 5.14. 'Grain of wheat' (κόκκος τοῦ σίτου) is set in quotation marks in the edition; it echoes both 1 Corinthians 15:37 (already quoted at 5.22) and John 12:24, so both are cited. 'Everything is possible to God' is the Christian saying Celsus mocks; the closest Gospel wording is Matthew 19:26 / Mark 10:27 (compare also Luke 1:37); cited as an allusion. λόγος τις in the body rendered 'a certain principle' (the seminal principle, as in 5.22); ἀφ᾿ οὗ kept as 'from this principle'. κατὰ λόγον θεοῦ rendered 'in accordance with God's reason', since it is set against ἀλόγως ('without reason'); not capitalised as the Word. παράδοξα rendered 'extraordinary'. βεβιασμένως ὀνομάσαι: 'use a forced term'. τῶν κατὰ περίοδον ἀπαραλλάκτων: the Stoic doctrine of identical recurrence in each world-cycle. 'God would be able not to be God' is a possible echo of 2 Timothy 2:13 ('he cannot deny himself'), not cited inline because the wording does not match. Koetschau 'τᾷ θεῷ' is a misprint for τῷ θεῷ in the staged text; no effect on sense. 'οὐ (γὰρ)': Koetschau's supplement, translated.
